'''''Osteospermum moniliferum''''' (synonym '''''Chrysanthemoides monilifera''''') is an evergreen flowering [[shrub]] or small tree in the daisy family, [[Asteraceae]]. It is native to southern Africa, ranging through South Africa and Lesotho to Mozambique and Zimbabwe.<ref name = powo/>

Most subspecies have woolly, dull, serrate, oval leaves, but the subspecies ''rotundatum'' has glossy round leaves. Subspecies are known as '''boneseed''' and '''bitou bush''' in Australasia,<ref name="Blood">{{Citation
 | last =Blood
 | first =K
 | year =2001
 | title =Environmental weeds: a field guide for SE Australia
 | location =Melbourne, Vic., Australia
 | publisher =CH Jerram & Associates
 | isbn =0-9579086-0-1
 | pages =46–47, 86
 | oclc =156877920
}}</ref> or '''bietou''', '''tick berry''', '''bosluisbessie''', or '''weskusbietou''' in South Africa.<ref name="vanJaarsveld">{{Citation

 |first=Ernst

}} (Archived by )</ref> The plant has become a major environmental weed and [[invasive species in Australia]] and New Zealand.<ref name="Blood" />

==Taxonomy==
''Osteospermum moniliferum'' has five recognized subspecies:<ref name=powo/>
*''Osteospermum moniliferum'' subsp. ''canescens'' {{small|(DC.) J.C.Manning & Goldblatt}}
*''Osteospermum moniliferum'' subsp. ''moniliferum''
*''Osteospermum moniliferum'' subsp. ''pisiferum'' {{small|(L.) J.C.Manning & Goldblatt}}
*''Osteospermum moniliferum'' subsp. ''rotundatum'' {{small|(DC.) J.C.Manning & Goldblatt}}
*''Osteospermum moniliferum'' subsp. ''septentrionale'' {{small|(Norl.) J.C.Manning & Goldblatt}}

''Osteospermum moniliferum'' was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753. It was given the [[binomial name]] ''Chrysanthemoides monilifera'' in 1943 by Nils Tycho Norlindh.<ref name="vanJaarsveld" /> It was one of two species in genus ''Chrysanthemoides'', along with ''Chrysanthemoides incana'' (now ''Osteospermum incanum'').<ref name="Scott">{{Citation

| bibcode =1996JApEc..33.1496S
 }}</ref>

The species name ''moniliferum'' comes from the [[Latin]], ''monile'', meaning necklace or collar, referring to the shiny fruit arranged around the flowers like a necklace.<ref name="vanJaarsveld" />

In [[Australia]], ''O. m.'' subsp. ''moniliferum'' is known by the common name 'boneseed', while ''O. m.'' subsp. ''rotundatum'' is known by the common name 'bitou bush'.<ref name="Brougham">{{Citation

==Description==
Boneseed is a perennial, woody, upright shrub, growing to {{convert|3|m|ft|abbr=on}},<ref name="CRC">{{Citation
 |last=CRC for Australian Weed Management 
 |year=2003 
 |title=Weed Management Guide – Boneseed - ''Chrysanthemoidesmonilifera'' ssp. ''monilifera'' 
 |pages=1–2 
 |url=http://www.weedscrc.org.au/documents/wmg_boneseed.pdf 
 |accessdate=2008-08-04 
 |url-status=dead 
 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080724080421/http://www.weedscrc.org.au/documents/wmg_boneseed.pdf 
 |archivedate=2008-07-24 
}} (Archived by the [https://web.archive.org/web/20070901013039/http://weeds.crc.org.au/documents/wmg_boneseed.pdf Wayback Machine])</ref> although occasionally taller.<ref name="Blood" /> It is a member of the ''Asteraceae'' (daisy) family and has showy, bright yellow [[flower]]s in swirls of 5–8 'petals' (ray florets) up to {{convert|30|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name="CRC" /> Fruit are berry-like, spherical at around 8 mm in diameter, and turn dark-brown to black with a bone-coloured seed inside of 6–7 mm diameter. Leaves are {{convert|2|–|6|cm|in|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|1.5|–|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide, oval tapering to the base with irregularly serrate margins.<ref name="Blood" />

Bitou bush can be distinguished from boneseed in part due to its more rounded sprawling habit to {{convert|1.5|–|2|m|ft|abbr=on}}, less noticeably toothy leaf margins and seeds that are egg-like rather than spherical.<ref name="Blood" /><ref name="Brougham" /><ref name="CRC" /><ref name="Auld">{{Citation
 | last1 =Auld
 | first1 =BA
 | last2 =Medd
 | first2 =RW
 | year =1992
 | title =Weeds: an illustrated botanical guide to the weeds of Australia
 | edition =Revised
 | location =Melbourne, Vic., Australia
 | publisher =Inkata Press
 | page =93
 | isbn =0-909605-37-8
 | oclc =16581672
}}</ref>

Both boneseed and bitou bush hybridise readily, however, so examples of plants demonstrating a fusion of traits is possible.<ref name="Blood" />

''O. moniliferum'' has been shown to need pollinators in order to reproduce.<ref name=":0" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Osteospermum moniliferum'' occurs naturally in coastal areas of [[South Africa]], reaching into [[Lesotho]], [[Zimbabwe]], and southern [[Mozambique]].<ref name = powo/>  Subspecies ''rotundatum'' is concentrated along the eastern coast of South Africa from its southern tip through [[KwaZulu-Natal]] to southern Mozambique.<ref name="Scott" /><ref>[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77132414-1 ''Osteospermum moniliferum'' subsp. ''rotundatum'' (DC.) J.C.Manning & Goldblatt]. ''[[Plants of the World Online]]''. Retrieved 29 September 2023.</ref> Subspecies ''moniliferum'' is concentrated around [[Cape Town]] and the [[Cape Peninsula]] on South Africa's south western coast, where its native [[habitat]]s include the [[Cape Flats Dune Strandveld]].<ref name="Scott" /> Subspecies ''canescens'' is native to Kwazulu-Natal, the [[Northern Provinces]], and [[Free State (province)|Free State]] of South Africa and to Lesotho.<ref>[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77132417-1 ''Osteospermum moniliferum'' subsp. ''canescens'' (DC.) J.C.Manning & Goldblatt]. ''[[Plants of the World Online]]''. Retrieved 29 September 2023.</ref> Subspecies ''septentrionale'' is native to Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and the Northern Provinces.<ref>[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77132419-1 ''Osteospermum moniliferum'' subsp. ''septentrionale'' (Norl.) J.C.Manning & Goldblatt]. ''[[Plants of the World Online]]''. Retrieved 29 September 2023.</ref>

==Invasive species==
[[File:CSIRO ScienceImage 1681 Boneseed Weed in the YouYangs Victoria.jpg|thumb|Boneseed in the [[You Yangs]], Victoria, Australia]]

===Australia===
{{Main|Boneseed in Australia}}
In Australia, subspecies ''rotundatum'' (bitou bush) has naturalised along the coast of [[Queensland]] and [[New South Wales]], while subspecies ''moniliferum'' (boneseed) has naturalised along and near the coast in parts of [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and [[South Australia]].<ref name="Brougham" />

===New Zealand===
In New Zealand ''O. moniliferum'', which is listed on the [[National Pest Plant Accord]], is common in coastal locations throughout the [[North Island]], and can also be found in the [[South Island]] in Nelson City, [[Port Hills]] ([[Christchurch]]) and the [[Otago Peninsula]].<ref name="Roy" />

==Impact==
In Australia, ''O. moniliferum'' has been particularly successful in invading natural bushland. In part, this is due to the species' ability to establish on relatively nutrient-poor soils<ref name="Parsons">{{Citation
 | last =Parsons
 | first =WT
 | year =1973
 | title =Noxious weeds of Victoria
 | location =Melbourne, Vic., Australia
 | publisher =Inkata Press
 | pages =100–101
 | isbn =0-909605-00-9
 | oclc =874633
}}</ref> and in areas exposed to salt such as coastlines, as well as the ability of the seeds to germinate readily.<ref name="CRC" /> Disturbances such as fire can assist ''O. moniliferum'' to spread as the plant produces a large amount of seed that can persist in the [[soil seed bank]] for 10 years or more, and this reserve in turn enables the species to quickly recolonize a burnt area.<ref name="Blood" />

An individual plant can produce 50,000 seeds a year, about 60% of which are viable.<ref name="CRC" /> Once germinated, seedlings grow vigorously with dense, bushy growth.<ref name="Parsons" /> This lush growth shades out and displaces slower growing native species that might otherwise occupy the same ecological niche.<ref name="Brougham" /> Rapid, vigorous growth also means that ''O. moniliferum'' is capable of flowering and setting seed within 12–18 months,<ref name="Parsons" /> making it extremely persistent even in situations where disturbance or regular management activity is common.

Once established, the plant's shallow root system enables it to absorb moisture after light rain before the moisture reaches the roots of more deeply rooted species<ref name="CRC" /> further limiting opportunities for slower growing species to establish and out-compete ''O. moniliferum'' over time. Furthermore, outside of Southern Africa the plant has few local, indigenous pathogens or predators to control its growth<ref name="Brougham" /> also reducing the potential for gaps to emerge that might provide opportunities for other species to reestablish. The net consequence of ''C. monilifera'''s growth characteristics is that outside of its natural ecosystem it can ultimately form large, dense, unhealthy stands of a single species with extraordinarily poor biodiversity.

The plant can extend its existing range in a variety of ways. Its fruit is attractive to birds, rabbits, other animals and even some insects such as ants, and because seeds are tough and difficult to digest they will often be dispersed in animal [[feces|droppings]].<ref name="Parsons" /><ref name="Emert">{{Citation
 | last =Emert
 | first =S
 | year =2001
 | title =Gardener's companion to weeds
 | edition =2nd
 | location =Sydney, NSW, Australia
 | publisher =Reed New Holland
 | page =100
 | isbn =1-876334-77-0
 | oclc =52245716
}}</ref> Seeds can also spread on vehicles and equipment, in contaminated soil, in garden waste, along water drainage lines and deliberately by human intervention.<ref name="Blood" />
''Osteospermum moniliferum'', unlike many other weed species, is not generally considered to be a problem for agricultural productivity due to its sensitivity to trampling as well as being readily grazed by stock.<ref name="CRC" /><ref name="Parsons" /><ref name="Emert" />

==Control==
''Osteospermum moniliferum'' is potentially susceptible to a range of control strategies, but Burgman and Lindenmayer recommended that the strategy chosen be responsive to the local situation and available resources.<ref name="Brougham" /> Due to its relatively shallow root system, removal by hand is an ideal method of control.<ref name="Brougham"/><ref name="Emert" /> Where manual removal is impractical, many common herbicides can be used, in which case the herbicide is commonly applied directly to the wood of the plant via a cut notch, or at the end of a pruned stump.<ref name="Brougham"/> Mechanical removal of ''O. moniliferum'' by tractor or other machinery can also be effective, but that process can be extremely indiscriminate, and is only recommended in areas of poor environmental values and minimal erosion risk.<ref name="Brougham"/>

Another way of tackling an infestation is the use of controlled burns, but there are risks associated with that method. Principally, ''O. moniliferum'' has higher moisture levels than many Australian indigenous species so, for burns to be effective, a burn of higher than normal intensity is required. That can, in turn, have a detrimental impact on indigenous vegetation which has evolved in response to more frequent, lower-intensity fires. Furthermore, fire can trigger re-germination from the extensive ''O. moniliferum'' seed bank, potentially worsening the situation. However, if a program is implemented to monitor and control ''C. monilifera'' seedlings following the burn and emerging ''O. moniliferum'' seedlings are removed, burning can be extremely effective at exhausting the seed bank and minimising the chances of re-infestation.<ref name="Brougham"/><ref name="CRC"/>

Various methods of biological control have been attempted, particularly the introduction of insects which are natural enemies of ''O. moniliferum'', such as the bitou tip moth (''[[Comostolopsis germana]]'') and bitou seed fly (''[[Mesoclanis polana]]'').<ref name="Brougham"/> Although they have had some success in controlling bitou bush (ssp. ''rotundatum'') in Australia, to date they have not had similar success in combating boneseed (ssp. ''moniliferum'').<ref name="Brougham"/>

In a study carried out by researchers at the [[University of New England (Australia)|University of New England]] and published in 2017, it was found that a serious error was made with the introduction of biological control agents into Australia for ''C. moniliferum'' ssp. ''rotundatum''. Bitou seed fly (''Mesoclanis polana'') was introduced based on the naive belief that it is a natural enemy of ''O. moniliferum.'' After reviewing many hours of video footage of bitou bush flowers in Northern NSW, researchers at the School of Ecosystem Management<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.une.edu.au/study/study-options/what-to-study/study-areas/animal-related-studies/ecosystem-management | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171222052955/https://www.une.edu.au/study/study-options/what-to-study/study-areas/animal-related-studies/ecosystem-management | archive-date=2017-12-22 | title=Ecosystem Management - University of New England (UNE) }}</ref> found that ''Mesoclanis polana'' is actually the most frequent pollinator of ''O. moniliferum''.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Gross|first1=Caroline L.|last2=Whitehead|first2=Joshua D. |last3=Silveira de Souza|first3=Camila|last4=Mackay|first4=David|date=2017-09-21|title=Unsuccessful introduced biocontrol agents can act as pollinators of invasive weeds: Bitou Bush (Chrysanthemoides monilifera ssp. rotundata) as an example|journal=Ecology and Evolution |volume=7 |issue=20|pages=8643–8656|doi=10.1002/ece3.3441|doi-access=free |issn=2045-7758|pmc=648678|pmid=29075478 |bibcode=2017EcoEv...7.8643G }}</ref> Because ''O. moniliferum'' is a weed of National Significance in Australia, that oversight could potentially be devastating to Australian ecosystems. Much like the introduction of the [[cane toad]] to control the population of [[Dermolepida albohirtum|cane beetles]], such a discovery is an important reminder about the importance of thoroughly researching biological control agents before introducing them into new ecosystems.
